podcast.title: Discovery of Little Richard
podcast.body: Specialty Records signed Little Richard after A&R head Bumps Blackwell, looking for a gospel-sounding R&B singer to compete with Ray Charles, heard Richard's demo tape. They bought Richard's contract from Peacock Records for $600. "Blackwell and Roup made an agreement with Don Roby to buy out his contract for $600."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Early Signings of Black Artists
podcast.body: Specialty Records was among the pioneering labels to sign and record black gospel acts like The Soul Stirrers in the late 1940s. "In the late 40s The Soul Sturlers signed to specialty records, one of the first acts to sign to the label"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Half-Rate Mechanical Licensing
podcast.body: Specialty Records, owned by Art Rupe, licensed songs like "Tutti Frutti" from a publishing company also owned by Art Rupe. This cross-collateralization meant Specialty only paid half the normal mechanical licensing rate (one cent per record instead of two cents), a common but frustrating practice for artists like Little Richard. "That company licensed the song to specialty records, for half the normal mechanical licensing rate."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Jesse Belvin's First Solo Contract
podcast.body: Jesse Belvin signed with Specialty Records for his first foray into a solo career after recording two singles with Big Jay McNeely's group, Three Dots and a Dash. His initial solo single, "Baby Don't Go," was not particularly successful on this label, leading to his subsequent collaboration with Marvin Phillips. "After recording two singles with McNally, Belvin went off to make his own records, signing to specialty records."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Release of Backlog After Little Richard's Hiatus
podcast.body: After Little Richard effectively stopped recording rock and roll due to his religious conversion, Specialty Records capitalized on his undiminished demand by releasing a substantial backlog of his recordings over the next couple of years, including chart-topping hits like "Good Golly Miss Molly" as well as substandard material initially not intended for release. "Whatever the truth, specialty had enough of a backlog of little Richard recordings that they could keep issuing them for the next couple of years."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Royalty Practices
podcast.body: Specialty Records, under Art Rupe, had a policy that artists should ideally receive no more than one cent per record sold, reflecting Rupe's aversion to what he perceived as "greed" from artists demanding higher royalties. "Why should he pay the artist more than one cent per record sold?"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Shift from Gospel to Secular Music
podcast.body: The label, initially known for its gospel releases, began refocusing towards more secular styles of black music after Lloyd Price's "Lordy Miss Claude" became its biggest hit, recognizing the greater commercial potential. "maybe he should refocus the label away from gospel and towards more secular styles of music."

podcast.title: Sonny Bono's Early Career
podcast.body: Sonny Bono worked as a young songwriter for Specialty Records, writing songs for artists such as Sam Cooke, Larry Williams, and Dillon Di. "Sonny Barrow was a young songwriter who had written songs its specialty records for people like Sam Cook, Larry Williams and Dolan Jui."

podcast.title: Source of R&B Influence
podcast.body: This label was known for recording artists such as Little Richard and Larry Williams, whose R&B music significantly influenced Richie Valens' early musical interests. "Valens' big interest in school was music, especially R&B, and especially the music of Little Richard and Larry Williams, and other people who had recorded for specialty records."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Unfavorable Contract Terms with Little Richard
podcast.body: Specialty Records' contract with Little Richard paid him only half a cent per record sold, which he considered "far too low," and its terms stipulated that the contract could only be terminated by his death or an "act of God." This led John Mariscalco to suggest Richard's religious conversion was an attempt to legally escape these terms. "Richard's contract with specialty was only paying him half a cent per record sold, which he considered far too low, and the wording of the contract only let him end it on either his own death or an act of God."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
